claims.text: Laser-induced thermionic-emission reduction is a nanosecond-pulsed synthesis route for high-entropy nanoalloys.
The laser route can produce high-entropy nanoalloys with particle sizes of approximately 1–3 nm.
High-entropy nanoalloys have equiatomic or near-equiatomic elemental ratios.
Slow reaction kinetics in conventional synthesis methods can lead to phase segregation during nanoalloy formation.
Conventionally synthesized high-entropy nanoalloys tend to segregate during prolonged high-temperature operation.
Nanosecond laser synthesis suppresses atomic diffusion.
Nanosecond laser synthesis suppresses phase nucleation.
The laser route dramatically shortens reduction and nucleation time relative to conventional synthesis.
Shortening reduction and nucleation time limits diffusion sufficiently to prevent thermodynamically driven segregation.
Laser synthesis produces a homogeneously mixed elemental distribution in high-entropy nanoalloys.
Laser-synthesized particles have fewer grain-boundary or surface diffusion pathways than conventionally synthesized particles.
Reduced grain-boundary or surface diffusion maintains a single-phase solid solution.
Kinetic freezing preserves the high configurational entropy of the nanoalloy.
Preservation of configurational entropy ensures chemical and structural stability at elevated temperatures.
The synthesis-time kinetic suppression continues to prevent the onset of elemental segregation during later high-temperature exposure.
After high-temperature exposure, laser-synthesized nanoalloys will retain a more uniform, single-phase elemental distribution than slow-route controls.
The prediction is bounded to particles approximately 1–3 nm in size and temperatures below their melting points.
Electronic interactions may provide an additional composition-dependent contribution to stability.
A lack of statistically significant improvement in phase homogeneity for the laser-synthesized samples relative to controls would falsify the proposed kinetic-stability mechanism.
